### Introduction

In the class activity, you tested a school board member's claim using data from Montgomery County, Pa. — and found a model that didn't hold up. Now you'll run the same analysis using data from Montgomery County, Md. Your job is to evaluate whether the Maryland data tells a different story, and what that means for how you'd report on the claim.

### Loading the Data

```{r}
schools <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405_files/refs/heads/main/montgomery_md.csv")
```

### Task 1: Examine the Data First (2 points)

Before you plot anything, look at the data — you know why by now.

```{r}
summary(schools$`FARMS Pct`)
schools |> arrange(desc(`FARMS Pct`)) |> head(10)
```

Are there any data quality issues like the ones you found in the Pennsylvania data? How does the distribution of FARMS percentages compare between the two counties? Note anything that concerns you or gives you confidence in the data.

Similarly to the data quality issues we found in the Pennsylvania data it seems that there is a large gap between Q3 and the Maximum as it jumps from 62 to 96. This means that the data is probably skewed again as the larger numbers are pulling the data to one side. Those in MOCO Maryland who are in the top percentage of FARMMS programs have a lower percentage of students meeting or exceeding math expectations in schools in comparison to the higher percentages that we saw in the MOCO Pennsylvania schools. I feel more confident in this data as there are no schools with 100% of their students in the FARMS program which makes the data more reliable unlike the Pennsylvania data. It does concern me that percentage of those students in the FARMS program are doing worse in meeting or exceeding math expectations. 

### Task 2: Create a Scatterplot and Compare (5 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME value with the correct variable name to create a scatterplot of FARMS percentage vs. math scores for Montgomery County, Md.

```{r}
schools |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `FARMS Pct`, y = `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "FARMS Percentage", y = "% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations",
       title = "Math Scores vs. FARMS Percentage, Montgomery County MD")
```

Describe what you see. Then compare this scatterplot specifically to the Pennsylvania one: what differences do you notice in the direction, strength, and spread of the relationship? The two counties share a name and are both suburban — what might explain why they look so different?

The data in this scatterplot shows that as the FARMS percentage goes up the percentage of students that met or exceeded math expectations goes down. The data in the Pennsylvania scatterplot slowly increases instead. The data in this scatterplot is alwso less spread out and is closer to the line of best fit in comparision to the Pennsylvania scatterplot. The data in the Pennsylvania scatterplot is also very clustered on one side of the plot whereas this scatterplot is significantly more spread out.The explanation of why the two might look so different is because of the different types of state curiculms for math test taking as well as just math classes in general. 

### Task 3: Linear Regression Model (5 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME value with the correct variable name to run a linear regression model predicting math scores from FARMS percentage.

```{r}
model <- lm(`% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations` ~ `FARMS Pct`, data = schools)
summary(model)
```

Report the three key statistics: the p-value, the Adjusted R-squared, and the coefficient for FARMS Pct. Then interpret them together — not separately. What does the combination of these three numbers tell you about the relationship between poverty and math scores in Montgomery County, Md.? Is this model worth using? How does it compare to the Pennsylvania model?

P-value of  0.00000000000000022 would indicate a significant result while the Pennsylvania model did not show significant result. The Adjusted R-squared value shows that the data represents about 67% variance in the math percentage of the FARMS figure while in the Pennsylvania model the 4% showed us that the math percentage of the FARMS figure only actually accounts for 4% which is quite low. The coefficient was -0.59511 which means that if you raise the FARMS percentage by 1% the math percentage decreases by 0.59511% so we need a big change to make only a little bit of change. There is a negative relationship between the students in poverty that are in the FARMS percentage and percentage of students that Met or Exceeded Math Expectations. This model is worth using as it seems more accurate than Pennsylvania data and shows a clearly insignificant relationship.  

### Task 4: Identifying Schools with the Biggest Residuals (6 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME values with the correct variable names to calculate predicted values, residuals, and absolute residuals for each school. Then arrange the schools in descending order of absolute residuals.

```{r}
schools <- schools |>
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(model),
    residual = `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations` - predicted,
    abs_residual = abs(residual)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs_residual))

head(schools |> select(1, `FARMS Pct`, `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations`, predicted, residual), 10)
```

Identify the school with the largest positive residual (doing much better than the model predicts) and the school with the largest negative residual (doing much worse). For each school, find its zip code and look it up on [CensusReporter.org](https://censusreporter.org).

For each of the two schools, answer:
- What does the demographic and economic profile of the zip code look like?
- Does anything in that profile help explain why the school is over- or under-performing the model?
- What would your first reporting question be to the principal of that school?
 Broad Acres Elementary: 
 Has an economic profile of $29,849 per capita income and $80,768 median household income. The demographics are 34.3 in median age with 53% of the population being male and 53% being hispanic, 25% black, 10% asian, and 9% white. 15.8% in the zip code are below the poverty line. As there are more people of minority backgrounds in the zip code of the school and a majority of the kids are participate in the FARMS program it would make sense why this school is over-preforming. My first question to their principal of the school would be are you teaching math differently in order to beat the odds that poverty is causing kids to fail when this seems to be the opposite case for this school. 

Stedwick Elementary
Has an economic profile of $45,834 per capita income and $98,542 median household income. The demographics are 37.9 in median age with 50% of the population being male and 33% being hispanic, 23% black, 14% asian, and 23% white. 12.8% in the zip code are below the poverty line. As there are more people of minority backgrounds in the zip code of the school and but there are less kids in the FARMS program and more white kids than in the other school which makes sense why this school is under-preforming. My first question to their principal of the school would be what are we missing from the data with regards to students math performance as the odds that poverty is not harming kids math scores is quite wrong.


### Task 5: Evaluate the Model and Write the Pitch (7 points)

You've now run this analysis on two counties. Return to the school board member's claim: that elementary schools with fewer students on free and reduced-price meals do better on standardized math tests.

Write a short story pitch of 4-6 sentences that addresses all of the following: Does the Maryland data support or contradict the claim? How does it compare to what you found in Pennsylvania? What would you ask the school board member if you called them for comment? And what's the most interesting specific finding from your residuals analysis: which school would you want to visit first, and why?
